articles.headline: Rust? What rust? Brewers open World Series refreshed and ready thanks to all that winning
keyFacts: The Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.
Manager Pat Murphy stated that the team stayed sharp during their long layoff by playing practice games and taking live at-bats.
The Brewers will continue the series needing four more wins to claim the championship against the Rays.
body: MILWAUKEE -- The Milwaukee Brewers won Game 1 of the World Series, 3-2, Friday night at American Family Field. It was their first win since Thursday, Oct. 15. They hadn't lost since then either, though; they had been off.

Any time a team has a long layoff in the postseason, we end up hearing the same tired song and dance. "Rust vs. Rest" is the succinct headline. The basic argument is that with baseball being a daily sport in the regular season, teams sitting around for multiple days between series -- or between the end of the regular season and the divisional series -- are at some sort of disadvantage because they'll come out rusty.
It's nonsense, of course.
One example obviously doesn't disprove a theory -- though we have several more and we'll get to those -- but the Brewers are doing their best to kill that narrative.

In the first inning of World Series Game 1 on Friday, Jackson Chourio led off with a single. Christian Yelich tripled him home and then scored on a William Contreras single. In the span of four batters, the team that spent seven full days without playing a game just scored two runs. Nick Martinez, on the mound for the Rays, wasn't great in the second half, but he was an All-Star this season and was coming off an outing in which he allowed only one run in more than five innings against the Guardians in the ALCS.

Was Contreras rusty? After that RBI single in the first, he threw out two runners trying to steal and nailed both of his ABS challenges. It sure seems like a rusty catcher wouldn't be so excellent behind the plate at judging balls and strikes.
"Contreras was unbelievable," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said after the game. "The two caught stealings, the ABS, the hits, calling the game.

" ... Now, we did not play great. You can look back and we made a baserunning mistake, we made an execution mistake. We made a defensive mistake. We weren't perfect. But after being off for some time, I'm pleased we came out in the first inning ready to go."

The wait between sweeping the Dodgers in the NLDS and Game 1 of the World Series wasn't the Brewers' only break. They have now played just nine games in 26 days. They've won eight of them. It sort of blows up that "rusty" argument, doesn't it?

As all teams with long layoffs do, the Brewers had plenty of practices. These days, that's not just swings off batting practice pitchers; Trajekt technology uses holograms of real pitchers and recreates everything about their pitches, including spin rate, velocity, movement, the works. The tech has gotten so good that players have started bypassing minor-league rehab assignments after injury absences and instead just getting back up to game speed using the Trajekt machines.
The Brewers also played practice games.

"We played baseball, that's how we prepared," Murphy said on Thursday before their team workout. "We went out there and played baseball every day, live at-bats. You can't recreate real, you know what I mean? It's a long layoff, and if we want to use it as an excuse, then let people use it as an excuse, but I refuse to do that."

I'm glad he said something about excuses, because some of the narratives we've seen used with teams after layoffs in the past are tantamount to excuse-making. When high-seeded teams lose a game or even a series, people love to cling to excuses instead of just accepting that baseball in small samples lends itself to variance.

Sure, we've heard former players making claims like your body doesn't adjust well to not playing games for multiple days after having played nearly every day for six months, and maybe they do feel that, but the numbers tell us otherwise.

The 2022 and 2023 Braves seemed to be the poster child for this under the current playoff format, which debuted in 2022. How many times did we hear about how unfair it was that the top two seeds were forced to sit around and get rusty while the lower seeds get to play meaningful baseball, giving them a supposed edge?
Rubbish. Utter rubbish.

That very argument ignored the top-seeded Astros in 2022. They got a bye and then swept the Mariners in the ALDS, waited a few more days off and then swept the Yankees in the ALCS. They had another long layoff before the World Series and then beat the Phillies six games. They went 11-2 in all, the best record in this iteration of the playoffs. If the Brewers sweep here, they'll beat it.

In the current playoff format, teams with at least five days of rest before Game 1 have gone 14-10 in Games 1. You might think 10 losses is too many, but that record is a 162-game pace of 95 wins, and these are obviously all games against playoff teams. The rested teams are good, not rusty.

Let's get back to the Brewers. They earned the spotlight just as they've been doing all playoffs and, really, nearly the entire season. They earned the rest during their bye by having the best record in baseball with 103 wins. They earned their days off before the NLCS by getting rid of the Padres in four games instead of five. They earned more than a week of rest before the World Series by taking out the two-time defending champion Dodgers in a four-game sweep.

We already discussed the offense and Contreras behind the plate, but the Brewers again played great defense overall. There was one misplay in center in the fourth inning, but it was on a hard line drive right at Garrett Mitchell and those are always difficult to judge. The scorekeeper ruled it a double anyway, not an error.

Jacob Misiorowski, who has now thrown more than 40 innings over his previous career-high workload, saw his velocity tick up over his season average. He hadn't pitched since Oct. 11 and got deeper into the game than his previous two playoff starts.

The Brewers are a team that shortens games with their bullpen, and while they have depth, they'd prefer to ride their three back-inning beasts in Abner Uribe, Aaron Ashby and Trevor Megill. With all that rest, that trio has been able to impact nearly every game. Those three combined for four innings of work to close down Game 1 and they'll likely all be available for a similar workload in Game 2. In fact, even if they combine for four innings again in Game 2, there's a day off before Game 3, so it wouldn't be surprising to see this exact formula for each of the first three games. Hell, they could do it in Game 4, too.
Murphy himself said the rest was good for his squad.

"We needed a little bit of a break," he said on Thursday. "It was an emotional series in L.A. Cross-country trip, all that. We had a few days where it was a little lighter, but then we've picked it up and gotten a lot of live ABs, but nothing simulates the game the way it is."

The rest is what is setting the Brewers up for what could well be a historic run. Again, they've only played nine games in the last 26 days, but that is because they played such great baseball that they earned their rest. Winning means rest, and rest means winning.

In order for the Rays to win the World Series, they'll now have to beat the Brewers four times in the next five or six games. To find the Brewers' last four losses, we'd have to go back to Sept. 13. They've gone 18-3 since then, despite having all those days off.
They didn't forget how to play baseball. They may just have forgotten how to lose.

articles.headline: Nobody can protect the ball against Dyson Daniels right now
keyFacts: Atlanta Hawks guard Dyson Daniels recorded 12 steals through the first two games of the season, setting a new league mark for this century.
Daniels tallied five steals in a win against Orlando and seven steals in a victory over Charlotte to help the Hawks start 2-0.
Daniels said opponents made costly mistakes by throwing the ball directly into his hands.
body: Atlanta Hawks guard Dyson Daniels is wasting no time reminding the NBA why he is considered one of the league's most disruptive perimeter defenders.

Through the first two games of the season, Daniels has already recorded an impressive 12 steals, demonstrating the defensive instincts, quick hands, and relentless effort that have made him a nightmare for opposing ball handlers.
While scoring performances typically dominate headlines around the NBA, Daniels is proving that defense can be just as impactful.
His ability to anticipate passing lanes, pressure opposing guards, and create turnovers has provided Atlanta with an important defensive presence early in the season.

For the Hawks, Daniels' production represents more than an impressive individual statistic. His defensive activity creates additional transition opportunities, allowing Atlanta to push the basketball and generate easier scoring chances.
Daniels recorded five steals in Atlanta's 132-125 season-opening victory over the Orlando Magic, finishing with 20 points, four rebounds, and three assists.
Daniels making case for defensive player of the year

He followed that performance with seven steals in Friday's dominant 128-81 victory over the Charlotte Hornets. Daniels also contributed 11 points, nine rebounds, and four assists as Atlanta improved to 2-0.
His 12 steals are the most by any NBA player through the first two games of a season this century.
Following Friday's victory, Daniels acknowledged that Charlotte made some costly mistakes.
"In this game they were just giving it to me, I'm not going to lie. They were throwing it in my hands," Daniels said.
The Australian guard's defensive performance is quickly becoming one of the biggest storylines surrounding Atlanta's undefeated start.
With Daniels leading the defensive charge, the Hawks are showing early signs of becoming a dangerous team in the Eastern Conference.
If Daniels maintains anything close to this production, another All-Defensive selection could be within reach.
For now, one thing is clear: opposing teams must be extremely careful whenever Daniels is guarding the basketball.

articles.headline: Harrison football wins Sectional 24 opener against Boonville
keyFacts: Harrison defeated Boonville 20-14 in the IHSAA Class 4A Sectional 24 opener on Friday.
Harrison coach Moe Sutton expressed dissatisfaction with his team's missed assignments and penalties despite the win.
Harrison advances to play Bedford North Lawrence on the road in the October 30 semifinal.
body: EVANSVILLE — Harrison and Boonville football put on a scoring display to open IHSAA Class 4A, Sectional 24 Friday, Oct. 23. Thirty-four points were put on the board at Romain Stadium in the first half as the Warriors led 20-14.
But in the second half, zero points were scored for either team.
It was not perfect, but the Warriors are moving on to play Bedford North Lawrence (7-3) on the road in the October 30 semifinal. It is Harrison’s second sectional win in as many seasons.
More: Heritage Hills football digs deep with 'elite' defensive effort in sectional victory
More: SW Indiana high school football sectional opener scores, updates
Perhaps, a turning point for the program.
“That’s one thing that this group can hang their hat on,” Harrison coach Moe Sutton said. “I’m happy to get out of here with the win.”
Dissatisfaction following a sectional win
As the answer may suggest, Sutton was dissatisfied with what he saw against Boonville. Missed assignments and penalties cost the Warriors at various points of the game.
It was a rough week of practice for Harrison in the lead up to the game, as Sutton said his group had just one good day.

In the team huddle after the game, Sutton told his team he knows they have more in them. He challenged his group; now it is on the Harrison players to show a higher sense of urgency in preparation for the sectional semifinal.
“All the coaches I had growing up will tell you, ‘You play like you practice, and you practice like you play,’” Sutton said. “It showed tonight.”
Boonville’s season is over. After going 4-6 in coach Jonathan Batts’ first season, the Pioneers finished with a 6-4 record.
Boonville dealt with injuries to key pieces down the stretch of the season. But the opportunity was there to advance as the game remained close throughout.

“Coming out of the half, our defense played their butts off holding Harrison scoreless,” Batts said. “We just struggled when it mattered. Credit coach Sutton and his team, that’s a hard-fought ball club right there.”
Boonville had its opportunities to score in the second half, but multiple drives were halted in Harrison territory.

In the third quarter, quarterback Beau Seiler threw an interception off a tipped pass that landed in Harrison defensive back Dre Sanders’ hands. Later on, Harrison’s defense got stops on fourth down to change possession.
Batts was emotional after the game, embracing players as they walked off the field for the last time representing the Pioneers.
Takeaways from Harrison’s 20-14 win over Boonville in tonight’s Sectional 24 QF. 🏈 pic.twitter.com/HFgCkHVMtx

— Markos Tsegaye (@10_Markos_) October 24, 2026 The program will continue without a talented senior class of 16 players. That includes key contributors offensively like running back Mason Jones, wide receiver Bradyn Egli and tight end Wyatt Seiler.
“This senior group, man, they mean a lot to me,” Batts said. “They fought till the end of that one right there. We came in here shorthanded, but those boys stepped up and they fought.”
Harrison football turning things around

While they were not the highlight of Sutton’s postgame thoughts, Harrison had some positives. The Warriors scored three rushing touchdowns from three different rushers: DK Rankin, Khi’shaun Brown and quarterback Anthony Bavone. Brown’s rush was certainly impressive. evading tacklers on his way into the end zone.
Bavone had a good one too, but his most pivotal carry came late in the fourth quarter to give his team the first down that would put the game out of reach.
Harrison has now won four of its last five games. Teams always want to be playing your best football of the season at this point, and the Warriors have been doing just that.
“We’re trying to turn it around,” Bavone said. “Everybody doubted me at the beginning of the season. What (are) they going to say now?”
Sutton is certain a performance like the one against Boonville will not be enough to defeat Bedford North Lawrence.
“We won, but it wasn’t the way I wanted it to look for us,” Sutton said. “We’ll be here (Saturday) at 8 a.m. as usual and get ready for Bedford.”
Markos Tsegaye is a sports reporter for the Courier & Press. He can be reached at mtsegaye@usatodayco.com. Follow him on X @10_Markos_.

articles.headline: J.J. Abrams’ Best Original Sci-Fi Movie Officially Finds a New Home on Streaming
keyFacts: The 2008 sci-fi monster movie Cloverfield is now streaming on Peacock, Paramount Plus, and Pluto TV.
J.J. Abrams conceived the film after wanting to create an intense original monster movie instead of traditional kaiju films.
The 85-minute film combines found-footage horror with a creature feature as a monster attacks New York City.
body: In early 2006, J.J. Abrams was in the midst of a generational run. Alias was about to end, Lost had become a cultural phenomenon, and Abrams was traveling the world promoting his directorial debut with Mission: Impossible 3. Somehow, Abrams was just getting started.

At Paramount’s 2007 San Diego Comic-Con panel, Abrams said that while promoting MI3 in Japan, he had visited a toy store with his son. He wanted Godzilla toys. Abrams wanted “our own monster,” something “insane and intense,” rather than King Kong, who he called “adorable.” So he decided to make a movie about one.

That’s how Cloverfield was born. Abrams tapped Lost writer Drew Goddard to write the script and longtime collaborator Matt Reeves to direct. The first teaser appeared before Transformers in July 2007. At Comic-Con, Abrams showed a poster of a beheaded Statue of Liberty looming over a smoky New York City. No title. No actors. Just a release date: Jan. 18, 2008. Keep in mind, this was the same panel that showed early footage from Iron Man, Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull, and Abrams’ live-action Star Trek.

Say what you will about some of his less-loved work, but Abrams knows how to generate hype and mystery. Cloverfield, newly streaming on Peacock (but also available on Paramount Plus and for free on Pluto TV), is worthy of both.
What is Cloverfield about?

The easiest way to describe Cloverfield is as a perfect marriage of found-footage horror like The Blair Witch Project and a kaiju creature feature. A big monster attacks New York City, but the film is told entirely through video footage recorded on a personal camcorder. That allows Cloverfield to do some clever things with its structure. It technically opens on cryptic and generic footage that tells us we’re looking at evidence obtained by the U.S. Department of Defense. It notes “multiple sightings” of a case designated as “Cloverfield” and that the camera was retrieved at the “incident site … formerly known as Central Park.”

Right away, this spells disaster, but then we see a charming little date between Rob (Michael Stahl-David) and Beth (Odette Annable) in New York City as they travel to Coney Island. The bulk of the movie takes place almost a month later as Rob prepares to leave New York for a new job in Japan. At a going-away party, his friends capture messages for him on the camcorder. Rob’s strained relationship with Beth hangs over the night. She heads home early, not the only one frustrated by how the night has unfolded. Little do they know, it's about to get a lot worse.
Then an explosion lights up the skyline, the city begins to unravel into chaos, and the partygoers set out to find Beth.

That setup gives Cloverfield a clever human scale. This is a Godzilla movie filtered through a handful of young adults trying to get across a city they know, with a camera they’re already using. When Rob and his friends first spot an explosion in the distance, they’re on a rooftop. Having lived in New York myself, I recognize the vibe: a casual night above the street, watching the city go by. Then the blast sends chunks of flaming debris hurtling toward them. The shock lands so well because the movie lets the moment start out so ordinary.
A shaky camera with a clear view of the story

The footage throughout Cloverfield is shaky. That style felt dated even in 2008, but that’s also the point. Cloverfield is coherent enough to keep the geography and the stakes clear, and its breakneck pace does wonders. At just 85 minutes, it has little time to get bogged down in the format’s limitations or anything that even remotely resembles mythology. We don’t ever really get a good look at the monster as it rampages through the city. Instead, the focus is on humans struggling to survive as explosions rock the surrounding city.

At one point early in the film, that severed head of the Statue of Liberty lands in the street nearby. Immediately, everybody whips out their phones and begins recording rather than, I don’t know, running away screaming. This sort of bizarre behavior is so much more likely in 2026 than it was in 2008, and seeing it then felt almost comical. Yet in hindsight, this particular Abrams choice feels particularly prescient.

In a similar fashion, Cloverfield’s biggest strain is kind of obvious: Why would you keep filming while a monster is tearing through Manhattan and doing so jeopardizes your own safety? Hud (T.J. Miller), the party’s designated cameraman, thinks he caught the monster on camera early on and just decides to keep recording. It’s a convenient reason, but it gives the footage a little purpose beyond the movie’s need for a camera. And as the crisis grows, that impulse to document the impossible starts to feel believable.

What stays with me most is that Rob and Beth’s relationship remains such an important part of the story without taking it over. His decision to leave New York for a new job has driven them apart, and it probably explains why he didn’t pursue a relationship after their one-night stand. The disaster gives them a reason to find each other again, and the film lets that romance tug at the heartstrings just enough. As they face the end together, their story adds an ache to the spectacle without slowing it down.

I love Cloverfield. I enjoy the other movies bearing its name, too, even if they don’t feel coherently connected in any legitimate way (and yes, that includes Cloverfield Paradox). But where do you even go after a found-footage movie that makes the Godzilla-style citywide rampage feel this immediate and personal? Cloverfield’s best trick is that it never gives us the whole picture. It just gives us enough to feel what it would be like to be there.

articles.headline: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
keyFacts: Police in Bavaria detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's former Alpine mountain retreat known as the Eagle's Nest.
Emergency personnel deployed about 200 workers to battle the blaze, though difficult terrain hindered firefighting efforts.
A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the detained suspect is connected to the fire.
body: - Published
Police in the south German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 (19:15 GMT) on Friday, and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Difficult terrain was hindering efforts to extinguish the blaze and it was still burning early on Saturday, police said, with some 200 emergency personnel deployed. There were no reports of injuries.
The Nazi dictator used the retreat, which lies above the town of Berchtesgaden, as a part-time seat of government and met commanders there to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941.
A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire.
Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
According to its official website, external, it is "also a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship".
During World War Two, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews.

articles.headline: Brewers survive chaotic ninth-inning replay drama to beat Rays in World Series opener
keyFacts: The Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.
Milwaukee pitcher Trevor Megill escaped a ninth-inning jam after a video review overturned an apparent game-ending double play.
Christian Yelich and William Contreras sparked an early two-run rally to help the Brewers secure the victory.
body: Trevor Megill struck out Jonny DeLuca with runners on second and third to escape a ninth-inning jam as the Milwaukee Brewers held on for a 3-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.

DeLuca’s strikeout came after Tampa Bay’s Liam Hicks had grounded into an apparent game-ending double play that was overturned after a video review. Replays showed that Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.

“You have a big range of emotions,” Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it.”
Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to earn the victory.
“Not perfect, but good enough to get a win,” he said.

Yelich hit a run-scoring triple to spark a two-run rally in the first inning that put the Brewers ahead for good and delighted a sellout crowd reveling in Milwaukee’s first World Series game since 1982. Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.

It was the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.
The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.
Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and had not put a runner on base since the sixth inning until mounting a comeback attempt in the ninth.

Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles off Megill. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put the potential tying run in scoring position with Rays slugger Junior Caminero at the plate. Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.
Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what was initially ruled a game-ending double play.
Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared – before the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.
A replay review determined Pratt’s right foot came off the bag as he caught Turang’s throw. Hicks was still out at first, but the Rays now had runners at second and third with the score 3-2.
“I thought Coop had him, and obviously I was wrong,” Misiorowski said.
Megill finally sealed the win as DeLuca struck out swinging.
“You just have to lock it back in,” Yelich said. “It’s the World Series – you have to do what you have to do to make things happen.”

By sweeping the two-time defending World Series champions, the Los Angeles Dodgers, in the National League Championship Series, the Brewers had time to set up their rotation the way they wanted by handing the Game 1 start to Misiorowski, the hard-throwing NL Cy Young Award favorite.
Misiorowski opened the game by throwing the fastest pitch ever delivered in a World Series, a 103.5mph ball to Yandy Díaz. The right-hander finished with a season-low three strikeouts.

While Milwaukee started with their ace, Tampa Bay countered with Nick Martinez to give two-time All-Star pitchers Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta an extra day of rest. Martinez struck out five and allowed two runs over five innings, but a slow start proved costly.

Chourio lined a single to right field on Martinez’s first pitch, and Yelich drove him home with a one-out triple to centre. DeLuca covered 85ft to track down Yelich’s drive but just missed making a diving catch as the ball glanced off his glove.

Yelich was batting third in the lineup for the first time since 3 August. The three-time All-Star and 2018 NL MVP posted the lowest on-base percentage (.315) and OPS (.692) of his career, but he has stepped up his game since being named the first team captain in franchise history during the final week of the regular season.
He was the seventh player to triple in his first World Series plate appearance, and the first since Kansas City’s Lynn Jones in 1985, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
Contreras knocked home Yelich with a line-drive single to left that was deflected by shortstop Taylor Walls with the infield playing in.
Tampa Bay got a run back in the fourth.

Aranda drew a leadoff walk and advanced to third when Caminero doubled on a one-out liner with a 112.7mph exit velocity that sailed over centre fielder Garrett Mitchell and off his outstretched glove. Aranda came home on Hicks’ groundout to the right side.
Milwaukee extended their lead to 3-1 in the seventh. Pratt drew a leadoff walk from Steven Matz and scored from second when Chourio greeted Kevin Kelly with a two-out single.
That insurance run proved critical.
“The guys settled in right away and did a great job,” Yelich said. “We still have a ways to go, but it’s nice to get that first one.”

articles.headline: Britt McHenry resigns from State Department after basketball game altercation: Report
keyFacts: State Department press adviser Britt McHenry resigned after a video of her dumping a drink on a fan at a basketball game went viral.
Page Six reported that McHenry's altercation began when she confronted a heckler saying terrible things about model Winnie Harlow.
ABC News reported that the State Department referred to McHenry's exit as an internal personnel matter.
body: State Department press adviser Britt McHenry has reportedly resigned from her role in the Trump administration after a video of an altercation between her and another fan at a Washington, D.C., basketball game went viral on social media.

A video of McHenry at a Washington Wizards game blew up on social media this week, as it depicted her dumping a drink on a fan and leaving the section while blowing kisses toward the people who were seated around her. TMZ obtained the video and shared it on X Thursday. It has received over 10 million views.

McHenry, a former ESPN and Fox News analyst, posted in early September that she had recently begun her role as a press adviser under Secretary of State Marco Rubio . She traveled with Rubio and the State Department communications team to the U.N. General Assembly in New York in her first month on the job.

According to Page Six , which broke the news of McHenry’s resignation, McHenry’s altercation began when a man in the crowd began heckling Milwaukee Bucks player Kyle Kuzma, who is dating model Winnie Harlow. The outlet, citing an anonymous source, said the man was saying “terrible” things about Harlow, which caused McHenry to tell the heckler to “ease up.”
The outlet reported that Britt was “forced to resign.”
‘SHE WAS BECOMING A DISTRACTION’: HOW KATIE ZACHARIA LOST THE WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY JOB IN FOUR DAYS
The Washington Examiner has reached out to the State Department for comment. ABC News reported that the State Department referred to her exit as an “internal personnel matter.”

This is the second top press official to leave the Trump administration within the past two weeks. Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was ousted from her role last week after just four days on the job.
