articles.headline: Trump's U.N. ambassador says Iran war could drag on for another year
keyFacts: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has substantially increased its efforts to target U.S. personnel abroad.
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz stated that the war with Iran could potentially last for another year.
The United Nations reported that time is running out to deliver aid to the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
- U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has told the Financial Times the could last another year, but Waltz said he hopes the Iranians "come to the table" before that.

- The price of Brent crude oil briefly crossed $117 a barrel Friday, its highest level during the war, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed to have disabled seven tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump of lying about attacks on ships to drive up oil prices before the U.S. midterm elections.
Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.

The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.

The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.

Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
U.S. to reduce staffing at 4 embassies in Middle East
The U.S. State Department says it will reduce staffing at four U.S. embassies in the Middle East, not including Saudi Arabia, where nonessential diplomats and family members earlier this week.

The staffing changes — driven by concerns that Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants may escalate rocket, missile and drone attacks around the region — will affect the embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, but do not entail an order to leave, the department said.
The embassies involved are all under what is known as "restricted operations" status that has already reduced the size of their personnel footprints. The embassies will remain open.

On Wednesday, a U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News that the U.S. military had been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
CBS/AP
Iranian president to meet with Putin next week in Moscow
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will travel to Moscow next week for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, according to a report by Reuters.
It hasn't been long since Pezeshkian spoke to Putin in person, but this will be the first meeting between the two in Russia during the ongoing war.
The two leaders met with each other on the sidelines of the Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan on Oct. 8. The two also met at a summit in Kyrgyzstan in September.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov visited Tehran earlier this week as the two sides continue to strengthen relations. Araghchi said Russia and Iran were closer than ever, despite President Trump saying Russia was doing little to help Iran a day prior.
U.N. sounds alarm on besieged Yemen city of Taiz
Time is running out to get aid into Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters who are preventing supplies from reaching Yemen's third-largest city, the United Nations said Friday.
Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government.
"Safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access is urgently needed so that essential supplies and life-saving assistance can reach people in need," said the U.N. humanitarian agency OCHA.
"It's 20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off," said OCHA spokesman Jens Laerke.
"We are seeing increasingly that the fighting makes it impossible for us to get in and impossible for people to get out," he told a press conference in Geneva.
Laerke said the dwindling water supply was a growing concern, as most residents depended on water brought in by trucks.
"With the roads closed and the diesel to run the trucks very scarce, water production in the city has fallen by about half," he said.
U.S. envoy leaves open possibility of striking Iran this weekend, despite Trump's prior midterm promise

A U.S. official left open the door for the possibility of a strike on Iran this weekend, despite President Trump previously saying there would be none before the midterm elections in less than two weeks.

"Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely," Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and point man on Syria, who does not have a direct role on Iran policy, told Israeli army radio in response to a question.
"(President Trump) is very clear. He's open and available and accessible to a deal and we've been at the table for months and months and months," Barrack said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections Tuesday, in recent days has repeatedly vowed to topple the clerical state in Iran, following two major bombing campaigns against Iran since last year.
Mr. Trump has also signaled an openness to resuming strikes on Iran after a long deadlock in diplomacy although he earlier said it would not happen before midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Earlier Friday, Mr. Trump repeated a common refrain that the U.S. could choose to end the war anytime it wants through a renewed military campaign, but could also let the country "wither" under sanctions.
AFP/CBS
European, Mideast foreign ministers push peace and diplomacy at Istanbul talks

Foreign ministers from eight European and Middle Eastern countries met in Istanbul on Friday in an unprecedented format, urging diplomacy and peaceful solutions to prevail across the Middle East as well as the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Ministers from Britain, France, Germany and Italy met counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt to discuss Hormuz — a crucial trade route blocked in the Iran war — as well as Yemen and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

At the heart of the talks was the situation in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, which is paralyzing global trade and driving up energy prices as well as the attacks on Saudi Arabia by Houthis from Yemen, allies of Tehran.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said a new escalation between Iran and the United States "would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices."
"The first thing this group of eight countries ... will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region," he told journalists.
Italy's Antonio Tajani said the regional problem cannot be solved "from a purely military standpoint."
Wall Street mostly loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices
Stocks slipped Friday on Wall Street under increasing pressure from rising oil prices.

The S&P 500 fell 0.2%, adding to its decline from a day before. The index is on track for a second-straight week of losses. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 550 points, or just over 1%, as of 11:50 a.m. Eastern time.
The Nasdaq composite rose 0.2%, bolstered by gains for several big tech stocks that also helped ease losses elsewhere.

Rising oil prices weighed heavily on the broader market, where three out of every four stocks within the benchmark S&P 500 index fell. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.5% to over $117. It has surged from less than $97 at the start of October and is now at its highest level since March.
Trump says U.S. could take all of Iran's oil: "We could take the whole country"
President Trump delivered a familiar message on Iran as he left the White House for a trip to rally voters in Florida, but also added the U.S. could take all of Iran's oil if we wanted to.
"Iran is not able to do much now. And we could, if we wanted to, just take all of the oil," Mr. Trump said. "We could take the whole country."
"And as you know, the Hormuz Strait is ours, and that's the way we'll keep it," the president added.

Mr. Trump was also asked about U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz saying the war with Iran could drag on for another year, while the president has said for months the war will end "very soon."
"We could end it very quickly," Mr. Trump said. "But Iran is a failing nation. We're taking all the oil out that we want."
"The question is, 'Do we want to finish it off or do we just want to let it wither?' Because we're getting everything we wanted," he said.
Tanker involved in UAE oil spill identified, analysts say
The tanker involved in an oil spill off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has been identified, according to analysts who spoke to the Reuters new agency.
Emirati authorities have not named the vessel, but Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, told Reuters the oil slick was coming from a vessel called the Gem No. 2.
Another analyst told the news agency that satellite imagery appears to show a large spill coming from the tanker.

"The slick is considerably larger, covering approximately 160 square km (60 square miles), and looks to be coming from the ship," Leon Moreland, a researcher at the Conflict and Environment Observatory, said.
"Furthermore, a slick this close to shore increases the chance it could impact nearby beaches and ecologically sensitive habitats," he said.
The Gem No. 2 was hit by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE on Oct. 9, shipping sources told Reuters.
No group claimed responsibility for the incident at the time, but maritime security sources told the news agency that it took place outside of the Strait of Hormuz.
Further escalation between Iran and the U.S. "would leave no winners," French foreign minister says
Any further escalation between Iran and the U.S. "would leave no winners," France's foreign minister said Friday.

Speaking to reporters in Istanbul after a meeting with foreign ministers from the U.K., Germany, Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, Jean-Noel Barrot said that "a further escalation between Iran and the United States would leave no winners and would likely have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices," according to remarks reported by the Reuters news agency.
UAE resident describes smelling gas after oil tanker spill
Residents in the north of the United Arab Emirates have described smelling gas after an oil spill off the country's coastline.
Many Emiratis have reported chemical smells on social media in recent days, including residents in northern districts of Dubai, the largest city in the UAE.
"For the past two days it smelled like 10 gas stations spilled their gas everywhere," a Sharjah resident told the AFP news agency, asking to remain anonymous.
"I was on my balcony and panicked thinking gas was leaking in my house and I will blow up everyone."
Emirati authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement Friday, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.

News of the spill came a day after Iran claimed to have struck four commercial vessels in Persian Gulf waters and said three others had hit sea mines in the region, though President Trump has accused Tehran of making up the incidents to drive up oil prices.
CBS/AFP
Iranian state TV claims movement of "non-compliant" vessels in Strait of Hormuz completely halted

Iranian state TV claimed Friday, citing an unnamed source close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy, that all movement of "non-compliant" vessels through the Strait of Hormuz had been completely halted following a series of Iranian attacks on ships and navigational support systems.

The report cited the source as saying that if U.S. military escorts and ship-to-ship transfers - all of which the Iranian regime refers to as "oil smuggling" - resumes, action against the vessels and technical systems supporting them will be "much more forceful."

Iran has repeatedly warned commercial ships not to use the long-established shipping lanes through the strait, through which about 20% of global oil supplies passed before the war. Tehran demands that all vessels seek authorization and use a northern route, close to its coast, and it has attacked ships for months that refuse.
The Trump administration, however, has encouraged shippers to use an alternative southern route, close to Oman, to avoid Iranian tolls.
Iran claimed Thursday to have struck four ships that used that route, and said three others hit sea mines in the U.S.-designated shipping lanes.
President Trump on Thursday dismissed Iranian claims about striking vessels as lies aimed at increasing global oil prices ahead of the looming U.S. midterm elections.
Both Iran and the U.S. have claimed at various times during the war to have completely halted traffic that violates their respective blockades of the waterway.
Iran's foreign minister calls Israel's relationship with the U.S. "parasitic"
Iran's foreign minister has called Israel's relationship with the United States "parasitic," citing alleged American taxpayer funding for missile defense in Israel.

"The U.S. has over the past three years spent $11 BILLION in taxpayer money on missile defense for Israel," Abbas Araghchi wrote Friday in a post on X, citing calculations by independent policy analyst Stephen Semler, who said he arrived at the number using Pentagon budget documents, media reports, and open-source intelligence.
CBS News has not been able to independently verify the figures.

Semler is the founder of the Security Policy Reform Institute, a think tank that, according to its website, is "driven by empiricism and guided by progressive values" to promote "the meaningful reform of U.S. foreign policy to break the cycle of endless war and serve the most pressing economic, social, and political needs of working-class Americans."

Araghchi also said the U.S. had "fired more interceptors defending Israel than Israel has," a claim supported by a Washington Post story from May that cited U.S. Defense Department data and U.S. officials.
"That is not a symbiotic relationship," Araghchi said. "It is a parasitic one."
UAE reports oil spill from tanker

The United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill from a tanker off its coast Friday, a day after Iran claimed to have struck four commercial vessels in Persian Gulf waters and said three others had hit sea mines in the region.
Emirati authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.
It said "teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation ... to limit environmental impacts," adding that Umm Al Quwain beaches had been closed.
Many residents in the north of the UAE have reported oil smells on social media in recent days, including residents in northern districts of Dubai.
Frequent attacks on ships have been reported in recent weeks near the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States.

The British maritime security UKMTO reported on Oct. 9 that a vessel was hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control. According to the maritime security company Vanguard, the vessel in question was the Panama-flagged oil tanker GEM NO.2.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed the seven additional incidents on Thursday, but none have been corroborated thus far, and President Trump accused Tehran of inventing strikes on ships to drive up oil prices.
CBS/AFP
Saudi Arabia postpones U.N. summit in Riyadh amid Houthi strikes
Saudi Arabia has postponed the sixth U.N. World Data Forum and the second Saudi Statistical Forum, which had been scheduled to take place in Riyadh next month, until 2027.
The kingdom's General Authority for Statistics said the delay was intended to ensure broad international participation.
It comes after the recent rescheduling of Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative, known as "Davos in the Desert," which was also pushed back to 2027 amid escalating regional tension and .
U.S. ambassador to the U.N. says Iran war could last another year
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has said the war with Iran could drag on for another year.
In an interview with the Financial Times published Friday, Waltz said the U.S. could still be fighting the war President Trump initially said would last "" 12 months from now.
Waltz told the FT the U.S. will not have achieved its key goals in Iran until the country disposes of its highly enriched uranium and accepts a "meaningful agreement on their domestic enrichment."
"I'm not going to put out hypotheticals. One would hope that they'll come to the table in a meaningful way before that," Waltz said, referring to the possibility of another year of war.

He added that Mr. Trump "and the U.S. Navy can maintain this blockade [on Iranian ports] for the foreseeable future," and said the administration was still "tightening" its economic pressure campaign against Iran.
Mr. Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have renewed their threats to launch new strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Foreign ministers from Europe and Gulf region to discuss Strait of Hormuz and Iran conflict

Foreign ministers from seven nations in Europe, the Middle East and elsewhere will hold talks in Istanbul Friday focused on the Strait of Hormuz and the interlinked crises in the Middle East, as well as the Ukraine war.

Ministers from the so-called E3 group – Britain, France and Germany – will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group, composed of Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, to discuss the Israel-Palestinian crisis, developments in Yemen and the Strait of Hormuz, and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, a Turkish foreign ministry source told AFP.

British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband's office said the talks would revolve around "the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia," as the in its decade-long civil war, which has flared up amid the U.S. war on Iran.

"Despite positive progress from the U.S. and regional partners, passage through the Strait remains under threat, with traffic through the waterway sharply down on pre-war levels," a U.K. foreign ministry statement said.

It said Miliband would "advocate for a diplomatic solution to the crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms" and stress "how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilizing the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal."
"The U.K. is stepping up to help stabilize the region, having this week committed RAF Typhoons to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks in their airspace," it added.
CBS/AFP
Saudi Aramco says volume bypassing Strait of Hormuz via pipeline has surged

The president of Saudi state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco, whose facilities have been targeted by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants repeatedly for weeks, says the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has more than tripled.
The East-West pipeline's capacity has surged from 2 million to 7 million barrels each day, President and CEO Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business.

Built in the early 1980s, the pipeline has played a crucial role in Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil amid disruption to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. It carries crude from Saudi oil fields and production facilities in the east, on the Persian Gulf, to the Yanbu oil terminal on the Saudi Red Sea coast on the other side of the vast kingdom, from which it can be shipped to global markets.

That route, which, unlike the Gulf, has two available exits, has also been threatened and attacked by the Houthis, who have vowed to stop Saudi shipments via the Red Sea's southern gateway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Nasser said Saudi Aramco has used drones to assess damage caused to infrastructure, including sites key to the East-West pipeline, by Houthi attacks, and to help with firefighting.
CBS/AP
Trump accuses Iran of lying about strikes on ships to drive up oil prices
As crude oil prices hit their highest levels since May, President Trump accused Iran on Thursday of lying about attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up global energy prices.

"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
Brent crude, the international standard for oil, hit $112 a barrel Thursday morning, its highest price since May 18.

Iran claimed to have struck four vessels in the Persian Gulf Thursday after they transited the Strait of Hormuz using a U.S.-endorsed route that Tehran rejects, and it said three others hit sea mines in the region after using the same shipping lanes. All of the ships were damaged along or after using southern shipping lanes in the strait near the Omani coast, which the Trump administration has insisted for weeks is open to traffic.

The U.S. military has escorted tankers out of the Persian Gulf using that route, boosting the quantity of oil leaving the region, but it is a costly process. Overall instability in the Middle East has kept energy prices high despite the recently increased supplies.

articles.headline: Trump and the MAGA enthusiasm strategy
keyFacts: President Donald Trump expressed confidence during a flight to Iowa that Republicans will win the House of Representatives, despite widespread predictions of a GOP defeat.
Trump dismissed his national job approval rating of 38.8% as fake and claimed his actual approval is around 60%, citing strong support from his political base.
Trump pointed to economic indicators like the stock market, manufacturing progress, and new tax cut proposals to make a case for Republican accomplishments.
body: TRUMP AND THE MAGA ENTHUSIASM STRATEGY. In a conversation on board Air Force One, bound for Sioux City, Iowa, and another midterm rally for Republican candidates, I asked President Donald Trump whether, despite the excitement he sees at his rallies, he thinks the GOP is going to lose the House. Instead of answering immediately, he asked what I thought. I said yes, I think the GOP is going to lose. But I hoped to hear his view on the widespread belief that House Republicans are headed for defeat.
“People say that,” Trump said. “I just don’t see it. There’s such enthusiasm. You’ll see, you’ll go there today.”
Recommended Stories

Indeed, the Sioux City rally, held at the airport, was raucous; the crowd was clearly stoked. Then the president pointed to several of his other rallies. “You saw last night?” he said, referring to a wildly enthusiastic rally in South Carolina. And then he mentioned his much-talked-about Oct. 13 trip to Alaska.

“I took him from losing to being ahead,” Trump said of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is fighting for reelection not only against a strong bid from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola but also against what is essentially a Democratic dirty trick by a man named “Dan Sullivan” who registered as a Republican to run in hopes of pulling votes away from the real Sen. Sullivan. Trump couldn’t believe that on the Alaska ballot the real and the fake Dan Sullivan appeared indistinguishable.

As we discussed how Republicans can win, Trump pointed to GOP redistricting efforts to flip some Democratic seats. “We have the advantage of picking up some seats, right?” he said. He then asked “How many?” I said five, or maybe 10. Trump responded with “Eight? Nine?” All those numbers, including mine, were a little higher than some recent predictions that the GOP redistricting work will backfire, and Republicans will pick up seats in the low single digits. But who knows?

“I might be wrong,” Trump told me. “The country’s never done better. People feel good. The gasoline’s a little high, but it’s coming down. You know, gasoline is lower than it was with Biden and Obama, and I got rid of the nuclear threat.”

Trump’s critics will scoff at his “never done better” claim, and at least some of his supporters might wince. Indeed, one could make the alternative argument that Trump was elected to do one big thing — bring down inflation — and inflation on a yearly basis was 3% when Trump took office in January 2025, and it is 3.7% today. That’s nowhere near where it was — 9.1% — in the worst of the Joe Biden years, but Trump promised it would go down, and it hasn’t.

On the other hand, there is the bill of particulars Trump offered voters in Sioux City and every other place he has held rallies. Look at the stock market, he told the crowd in Iowa, and look at your 401(k). They’re both up. Then: “Income for hardworking Americans has soared to the highest level ever recorded.” That’s true. And then: “The poverty rate has just reached its best level in American history.” That’s true, too, referring to the period in which the rate has been recorded. Then Trump cited other improvements, in manufacturing and exports, some of which were overstated but did indeed reflect progress under Trump. In addition, for Iowa specifically, on Sept. 30 Trump announced the planned construction of a huge new steel plant in the state, which outgoing Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds called “transformational.”

“You just heard six statistics,” Trump told the crowd, resting his case. “Ladies and gentlemen, goodnight. I love Iowa very much. I’m leaving. How the hell can I beat it?” Trump jokingly started to walk offstage, his work done, while the audience cheered.

Say what you want, but that’s not nothing. At his rallies, Trump presents a compelling case for solid economic accomplishments — to go along with the higher energy and food prices that have made inflation so stubborn in the months after Trump started the war in Iran. He promises, of course, that gas prices will plunge as soon as the war ends, which he thinks will be after the midterm elections. That will be great if it happens, although until then prices will remain a real problem. Still, the good indicators in the economy are real.

So are Trump’s tax cuts. Onstage in Sioux City, he polled the crowd on their opinion of his moves to eliminate taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security. Reflecting the area’s economic and demographic makeup, no tax on tips was somewhat popular; no tax on overtime was more popular; and no tax on Social Security was really, really popular.

All of this, good and bad, factors into Trump’s job approval rating, which stands at 38.8% approval and 60.4% disapproval, according to the RealClearPolitics average of polls. A president’s job approval rating is one of the best predictors of his party’s midterm results, and Trump’s is, for Republicans, dangerously low.

I asked him about the job approval number. “It’s fake,” he quickly said. “It’s fake.” He pointed to the New York Times’s use of phony “Wedgewood” polls. That was a moment of real embarrassment for the paper, even though the New York Times said it did not use “Wedgewood” polls in calculating the president’s job approval rating. Nevertheless, Trump made the fake poll part of a larger indictment of polling. “The job approval, they said it’s 37, 38?” he asked incredulously. “I’m not at 38.”
I asked where he thought his approval rating actually stands. “I don’t believe I could be beaten by anybody,” Trump said. “I think that if I needed it, which I don’t, I think 60.”

What does that mean? Trump would say it means what he says — that his real job approval rating is 60%. I asked if he meant that he would be at 60 if he were running for office himself. “Yeah, I think I’d be in the 60s now,” he said. “Now, in the Republican Party, I’m way up. Show him the 99%. Have you seen it?”

By that last part, Trump was asking an aide to show me a video clip that he is fond of playing, of CNN’s Harry Enten, from Sept. 27, in which Enten said, “In the 2024 election versus Kamala Harris, [Trump] got 99% of the MAGA GOP vote. Perhaps surprisingly, I might have thought it would be 100%, but it was 99%. Compare that to his approval rating now with the MAGA GOP. It’s 98%.”

Put those numbers together with Trump’s experiences at his rallies, where he addresses large, enthusiastic crowds, and then add to that the persuasive fact that he has twice been elected president of the United States — add that all together and it accounts for Trump’s belief in his own popularity and ability to influence elections, even those in which he is not running.

I asked, “Do you ever think that you get such big, adoring crowds, and it’s almost like a bubble? Do you think, These 10,000 people, man, they love me, but the larger electorate, I’ve got to win their votes. I mean, there are independents out there?”

“I always cater to my base,” Trump said. “My base is big. I think my base is close to 100% of the Republican Party. … I think I’m close to 100. … It’s not MAGA, it’s just —.” At that moment, I interjected, “But it’s not the whole Republican Party.” Trump answered: “I think it’s close. I think the Bushes have largely faded. They’re gone.”

That’s certainly true. But the bottom line is that Trump sometimes views his Republican base as if it is the electorate as a whole. He draws impressive crowds made up of supporters who love him. He spends much of his time among people who revere him. Viewed from that perspective, a job approval rating of 38.8% just doesn’t make any sense.

If you start with Trump’s belief that economic indicators are strong for coming growth, and add his skepticism of polls, and then throw in his confidence in his sky-high, rock-solid approval ratings among his MAGA base — together, they add up to Trump’s belief that Republicans can win not just the Senate, which many observers see as too close to call right now, but the House, too, which those observers believe is lost to the GOP.

Trump knows the polls, of course. He is a close and discriminating reader of news stories. And he has certainly heard advisers, consultants, and others describe the adverse conditions Republicans face in races across the country. But what should he do? Tell his party that they’re going to lose? Trump knows how many Republicans look to him for leadership. If he appears to lose hope, they will, too. So he keeps at it as he nears the end of an extraordinary 32-day cross-country campaign tour. And he has a case to make.

articles.headline: El-Sayed refuses to answer questions about Muslim Brotherhood letter: ‘I’m not interested’
keyFacts: Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed interrupted a Fox News interview when asked about a 2012 letter he signed addressed to Egypt's Muslim Brotherhood leader.
El-Sayed stated that his loyalty is to the United States Constitution and denied ever being a member of the Muslim Brotherhood.
Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers argued that El-Sayed failed to properly disavow the Muslim Brotherhood during the contentious interview.
body: Abdul El-Sayed tried to shut down Bret Baier Friday as the Fox News host attempted to ask the Michigan Senate hopeful a question about the Muslim Brotherhood.

The polarizing Democrat immediately got defensive and repeatedly interrupted Baier during an interview on “Special Report” as the newsman pressed him on a 2012 letter addressed to the leader of the extremist group in Egypt that was signed by El-Sayed.
“Bret, Bret … no, no, no … let me just stop there,” El-Sayed interjected, cutting off Baier before he could finish the question.
“You are asking this question to raise the question about whether or not I have dual loyalty,” the former public health official assumed.
Baier shot back: “I’m not, this is specific.”
“My loyalty will be to the Constitution of the United States, and as as every senator who’s ever served, I will swear an oath to that Constitution,” El-Sayed said, interrupting the host again.
Undeterred, Baier attempted to ask the question once more, but El-Sayed, again, started talking over the journalist.
“I’m not interested in anything you’re going to pull out from a 2012 statement, a letter, you’re going to pull that out of context, you’re going to ask questions about my allegiance,” he said.
“Don’t be Rogers’ campaign. Be a journalist,” El-Sayed snapped.

“So as a journalist,” he told Baier condescendingly, “if you’re asking the question about my allegiance to the Constitution: I have never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. I never will be a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. I am interested in serving the United States. I’m interested in swearing an oath to the Constitution that every senator has sworn oath to.”

The 2012 letter, signed by El-Sayed and more than 30 others, urged Mohamed Morsi, the then-newly crowned president of Egypt and a leader in the Muslim Brotherhood, to “purge” the media and police, the Washington Free Beacon first reported last month.
The letter was published on Egyptian news site Al-Ahram Gate and was followed by a cruel crackdown on journalists in Egypt by Morsi’s government.
In a separate interview with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, the former congressman argued that El-Sayed didn’t “disavow” the Muslim Brotherhood in his contentious conversation with Baier.
“He’s been dancing around this issue for a while,” Rogers said.

“When you support an organization and say you’re going to purge the press and purge the police, not to say it, encourage them to do it … he has adopted the ideology of the Muslim Brotherhood,” the Republican argued.
The Muslim Brotherhood is a designated terrorist organization by Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — but not the US.
The group is controversial in part because of its radical offshoots such as Hamas.

articles.headline: Democrat James Talarico targets Elon Musk at rally: ‘Texas is not for sale’
keyFacts: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico held a campaign rally accusing Elon Musk of trying to buy the Senate race for Ken Paxton.
Federal filings show Elon Musk contributed 158 million dollars to a super PAC supporting Republican candidate Ken Paxton.
Early voting has begun with polls showing Talarico holding a narrow lead over Paxton ahead of the November election.
body: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has taken aim at Elon Musk, warning that the tech mogul is trying to buy political influence and declaring: “Texas is not for sale.”

Talarico held a campaign rally on Friday at the University of Texas at Austin, packing an auditorium at his alma mater with hundreds of students and other supporters, who cheered, whooped and waved campaign signs.

The Presbyterian seminarian’s insurgent run against Texas attorney general Ken Paxton – a staunch ally of Donald Trump – has become one of the most closely watched races in next month’s midterm elections to decide control of Congress. Democrats are seeking their first statewide win since 1994.

Talarico, 37, struck his usual upbeat message on Friday but also pulled no punches in denouncing Paxton – who was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and had a very public divorce – as the most corrupt politician in the state’s history.

“I have a legislative record; Ken Paxton has a criminal record,” said Talarico, a state representative, wearing a dark blue jacket, white open collar shirt and blue jeans. “This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or who puts money in their own. This election is about whether you want a senator who is for Texas or for himself. This election is about whether you want senator who serves you or serves their billionaire mega donors.”

Paxton, he continued, has the ultimate mega donor. “Elon Musk is trying to buy the Senate seat. We just found out that the richest man in the world is almost single-handedly bankrolling this effort to install Ken Paxton in the US Senate and stop the movement that we are building in our state.

“In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your screens, that was Elon. If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you received a text message saying scary things about me with scary black and white photos, that was Elon too.”

Speaking against the backdrop of a giant Texan state flag and 40 young supporters holding “Talarico” signs, the Democrat said that, where his movement is funded by 1.3 million individuals, Paxton is funded by “one dude”.

In a state where data centres have become an incendiary issue, Talarico said: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas. But on November 3rd, we are going to deliver a crystal clear message to the world’s first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale.”

Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X and other businesses there, has contributed $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund, which in turn transferred the same amount to Texas PAC, a Republican super PAC supporting Paxton, according to federal filings.

Talarico has offset the outside-spending disadvantage with grassroots fundraising. His campaign says it raised $64m from July through September, more than triple Paxton’s total, with 97% of donations under $100 each.

Talarico told the crowd that super PACs and “billionaire mega-donors” are spending $200m in the most expensive Senate race in US history to defeat his grassroots campaign. “Big money is powerful, but it is nothing compared to people power,” he insisted, invoking biblical imagery comparing his supporters to “the slingshot” that David used to defeat Goliath
Talarico’s rally capped a turbulent month in what has emerged as America’s biggest battleground state. Talarico fell ill with the flu at the end of September and was not seen in public for nine days.

At a rally in San Antonio, Texas, Donald Trump claimed without evidence that “Tala-freako”, as he nicknames the Democrat, is vegan and had fallen ill because he tried eating meat for political purposes. That quickly metastasised into an online rumour that Talarico had checked into a mental health facility in Ohio. It was comprehensively debunked.

Meanwhile the Wall Street Journal published a video showing Paxton celebrating New Year’s Eve in Dubai with two US fugitives, Anosh Ahmed and Sameer Suhail, who were indicted in Illinois on healthcare-fraud charges. Ahmed donated $190,000 to Paxton, including $25,000 after his indictment.
Back on the campaign trail, Talarico set out on a “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts” tour of the state. He held a CNN town hall with sceptical Republicans and independent voters.

Paxton, meanwhile, launched an 18-day bus tour of Texas. His message was aimed at conservative voters with the slogan “Come and Take It”, an attack on what he called the far left. Republicans sought to tie Talarico with positions on transgender issues that have proved potent in conservative campaigning.

The campaign entered its final stretch with the Democrat holding a narrow polling advantage. The RealClearPolitics average for polls conducted from 6 to 19 October put Talarico ahead by 1.8 percentage points. An Emerson College Polling/ Nexstar Media survey released on Thursday found that 48% of voters support Talarico while 46% favour Paxton.
Early voting began on 19 October, giving both campaigns an immediate test of their ability to mobilise supporters. Talarico voted earlier on Friday.

Supporters at Friday’s rally expressed growing frustration with incumbent Republican officials such as Paxton along with optimism that Talarico’s message could signal a new political era for the Lone Star State.
Alina Anil, a 19-year-old student at the University of Texas, who had already cast her ballot, said she attended the event to see Talarico in person and demonstrate her support.

“We’ve been red for a long time and nothing has really come out of it,” Anil said. “As a student, I don’t think there’s been a lot of changes in Texas. We need some change and James Talarico seems promising. He was a teacher before, so I have faith in that and I have faith in him.”

Dakota Walker, 31, a pediatric physical therapist, arrived wearing a custom T-shirt reading “Talafrico: Talarico refreshing for Texas”, in the style of the Topo-Chico brand of sparkling mineral water.
“What’s not to like about him, what’s not to love about him, honestly?” Walker said. “He has morals, he has values, he’s an overall good human being and I think we need a drastic change.

“I have to spend so much of my time fighting for my kids, making sure that they get what they need when a family with a child with a disability or different abilities shouldn’t have to do that. I know we need healthcare reform and he is very big on that.”
Texas Democrats have had their hopes dashed before, notably when former congressman Beto O’Rourke lost a race to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018 by less than 3 percentage points.
Asked what a Democratic statewide victory would mean, Walker replied: “Oh man, I’ll probably cry, honestly. We need a lot of change and I feel like it’s time for a new era.”

Patrick Pearson, 46, an assistive technology professional, said he wanted to back Talarico because of his commitment to policy change. “From everything I’ve read about him and heard, I think he sounds really awesome,” Pearson said. “He’s actually trying to make a change and has a very positive message.”

articles.headline: Avengers: Doomsday Promoted With Baseball-Themed Crossover Featuring MLB Players During World Series
keyFacts: Marvel Studios debuted a promotional crossover ad for Avengers: Doomsday featuring MLB players during Game 1 of the 2026 World Series.
The baseball-themed promo featured characters like Mr. Fantastic and The Thing before Dr. Doom attacked from the sky.
Avengers: Doomsday is scheduled to arrive in theaters everywhere on December 18.
body: Marvel Studios debuted a unique promo for Avengers: Doomsday during Game 1 of the 2026 World Series on Fox tonight between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. The ad is an Avengers-MLB crossover set on Earth-828 at Ebbets Field (the former home of the Dodgers when they were in Brooklyn; it was torn down on our Earth in 1960 – the promo is seemingly set in the same time period as The Fantastic Four: First Steps, as you can see New York Giants players in the background).

In it, Mr. Fantastic, sporting a Brooklyn Dodgers cap, takes the mound to throw a stretchy-armed first pitch while The Thing hypes up the players as current, modern MLB players Freddie Freeman, Jacob Misiorowski, Bryce Harper, Randy Arozarena, and Junior Caminero look on from the sidelines. They're interrupted when Dr. Doom attacks from the sky, with clips from the film interspersed throughout the promo.

Worlds collide ⚾An exclusive preview of Marvel's new Avengers movie assembles Bryce Harper, Freddie Freeman, Jacob Misiorowski, Junior Caminero and Randy Arozarena 👀Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters everywhere December 18 https://t.co/WX1YtKjAKt

— MLB (@MLB) October 24, 2026 Live sporting events, such as the Super Bowl, NBA Finals, and World Series remain one of Hollywood's favorite mediums to debut new trailers and promote films, as in the age of streaming and on-demand content, they're one of the few forms of programming that consistently drive a live, tuned-in audience.

Avengers: Doomsday returns Chris Evans as Steve Rogers (which is referenced in a clip from the film used in the MLB promo), while Robert Downey Jr. trades Iron Man's mask for Dr. Doom's and appears to be abducting heroes in the upcoming film (though we will see RDJ as Stark at least one more time, starting in 2028 at Disney California Adventure's upcoming Avengers: Infinity Defense ride ). Much of it remains shrouded in mystery, such that even actors in the film don't know what happens .

Audience interest appears to be strong, as ticket pre-sales are outpacing those of this summer's blockbuster hit Spider-Man: Brand New Day. But Marvel recommends you do your homework before heading to the theater for Doomsday.

articles.headline: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
keyFacts: The UK government announced a 100 million pound investment in a national AI Biosecurity Lab to strengthen defences against biological threats.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan stated the new lab will bring together scientific expertise to safeguard citizens from emerging risks.
OpenAI and Anthropic will support the lab by providing 200 million pounds worth of AI model credits.
body: - Published
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.
As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit Â£100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.
The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.
"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.
"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.
"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."
The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.
"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.
"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."
The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing Â£200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.
The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional Â£120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).

Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.

The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.

It will come alongside a Â£60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and Â£70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.

It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.

Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.
There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.
But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

articles.headline: Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 Review: A Dolphin Dive in the Right Direction
keyFacts: Developer Infinity Ward created Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 as a welcome improvement over previous sloppy series entries.
The single-player campaign features cinematic action and a new extraction shooter mode called DMZ replaces Zombies.
Modern Warfare 4 removes the omnimovement system for a slightly slower and heavier multiplayer experience.
body: The Call of Duty series needed a win this year. Last year’s Black Ops 7 was a clown car of bad decisions, featuring an always-online campaign mode with ridiculous zombie bosses and open-world Warzone. Worse still, the multiplayer mode (the only reason that many people buy the game) was entirely forgettable. Developer Treyarch was tasked with putting out Call of Duty games two years in a row — that crunch was a recipe for disaster.

On the other hand, that means Modern Warfare developer Infinity Ward had plenty of time to cook up the fourth and final entry in its own series. Thankfully, the studio used that extra runway to its advantage. Modern Warfare 4 may not have returned Call of Duty to the highest highs of the original trilogy that ended in 2009 (and which Infinity Ward rebooted over the last decade), but this is a leap in the right direction for a series that has become increasingly sloppy in recent years.
Players will find plenty of cinematic action in the single-player campaign, and the multiplayer mode has slowed down just a touch, which I think the game largely benefits from.
More from CNET

More importantly, Modern Warfare Zombies has been completely dropped in favor of DMZ, an accessible player-versus-player-versus-AI extraction shooter experience. The experimental swing feels like a lifeline for the series, and DMZ is the standout mode for the game.
The campaign identity crisis is (mostly) resolved
Modern Warfare 4 is a tighter game than Infinity Ward’s previous project, and it’s leagues better than Black Ops 7.

At the same time, it has a complicated campaign to crack open (and not because the plot is hard to follow). Players flit back and forth between the perspective of Captain John Price, longtime protagonist of the series, and South Korean soldier Park Hyun-Jun, a newcomer whose squad is fighting for his homeland. A battle rages against a united coalition of Russian and North Korean ultranationalists, who are blazing a path into other territories.

Russian bad actors have been the primary antagonists of every Modern Warfare game, and it’s actually really cool to see South Korea’s positive representation in a Call of Duty title. But the propaganda is laid on thick — Russia and North Korea are presented as sneering colonialist powers, while the Western world’s soldiers are a shield on every front.

Americans spearhead the fight against imperialism; forget about the Strait of Hormuz and gun down these unambiguously bad guys. The whole plot hinges on a somehow less-subtle Red Dawn-type of scenario, and the gung-ho military politics are absolutely nauseating this time around. Sure, Price is framed as morally gray — he’s working with a cartel to achieve his goals, and there’s boring melodrama where he comes to blows with his former allies — but he’s vindicated in the end because he is the type of Call of Duty leader that prevents global conflict.

Modern Warfare 4 also features an obligatory shockingly graphic mission, which is something of a tradition for the series. In it, you play as a North Korean soldier rounding up and executing the occupants of a small village for hiding a defector. During my playthrough, I earned an achievement for successfully interrogating a villager without beating them down. The whole affair is gratuitous, gross and gamified in a problematic way, exacerbated by the bizarre decision to continue making this kind of mission a mainstay in each game.

It’s a shame that the story is so trite and icky because the tentpole action is really good. The best mission takes place early in the campaign, when Price infiltrates a New York nightclub to search for a Russian oligarch. Bright lights and pulsing music contrast with brutal fistfights and gunplay — it’s like playing through the climax of a John Wick film. From there, the highlights keep coming: There’s a fight in a train yard where the cover moves on rails, a chase scene across Mumbai rooftops, a high-stakes nighttime penthouse raid and a full-out assault on a dictator’s compound.

But the worst mission in the campaign repeats the mistakes of other modern Call of Duty games. When the player’s squad initially counterattacks North Korean airspace, they’re shot down and have to survive behind enemy lines with scavenged gear. It’s an interesting setup that is completely wasted on a Warzone-like, open-world mission with a checklist of more than 50 optional collectibles to seek out.

The few puzzles that exist are mind-numbingly easy — despite my best efforts, I checked out after completing around half of the activities. I focused on the main objective to end the mission as soon as possible, which is just about the worst feeling to have while playing a game.

I don’t know if there’s an edict from up top to put one of these open-world missions in each new game to funnel players into Warzone, but they don’t work at all and are the worst part of any campaign.

Still, the folks that play the campaign will probably have a good time here. Players can explore tons of cool locales, and the enemies are surprisingly difficult this time around. Still, if you care about the loose narrative implications of a Call of Duty campaign, it’s tough to wash the bad taste out of your mouth.
DMZ is better than Warzone and a welcome reprieve from Zombies

DMZ, a fairly accessible extraction shooter game mode, returns with new content for the first time since its “beta” ended in 2023. Players have been mourning what could have been for years, but it seems like the developers at Infinity Ward have been tinkering with it in the background for quite some time.
And their hard work has paid off because I’m confident that DMZ is the standout mode for Modern Warfare 4.
This extraction shooter is perhaps simpler than even ARC Raiders, but that’s part of the appeal. Players drop into North Korea to loot, fight each other and take down key targets throughout the map.

Everything is streamlined and easy to understand, including the loot. During play, you will come across several types of scrap, an assortment of healing items and tons of weapons, so you don’t have to think too hard about what to grab. Just move, shoot and pull out high-value items, then run the loop again.

The enemy AI is surprisingly aggressive and fun to battle against, especially when you run into an overwhelming number of troops. Armored vehicles and helicopters will try to smear you into the dirt. It’s an adrenaline rush, and as far as I’m concerned, Infinity Ward nailed the really important part of DMZ. It’s tough to get the player-versus-AI balance right, but these enemies feel like a real threat.

Other players might also come for your loot, which is what sometimes puts folks off of the extraction genre altogether. But DMZ’s in-depth bounty system provides a foil to player-versus-player gameplay.

Folks who hunt down other players rack up a bounty and appear on the map, so pacifists have a better chance to steer clear while bounty hunters stalk them down. It’s a pretty genius compromise that encourages the player-versus-player enjoyers to butt heads while the player-versus-environment crowd hides away because the tension of a potential run-in with aggressors is never truly alleviated.

I’m concerned that the pared-down simplicity of the gameplay loop could hurt DMZ’s long-term success, but Infinity Ward seems committed to adding new world bosses. That could really shake up how matches play out, even if there’s nothing as over-the-top as Marathon’s Cryo Archive boss.

DMZ isn’t perfect, but I see the groundwork laid for one of the better extraction shooters I’ve played. Depending on how the development team builds on this game mode, I can see it becoming something special (and maybe even a Call of Duty mainstay for years to come).
Multiplayer remains quick, but it’s heavier and grounded
Call me an oldhead, I don’t care: Black Ops 7’s omnimovement system, which allowed players to run, jump and slide around while looking in any direction, was disastrous for Call of Duty game balance.

Treyarch’s update to the formula might work for massive Warzone maps where there’s plenty of open space and a higher time-to-kill for other players, but the smaller multiplayer maps become impossible to breathe on. Call of Duty is, first and foremost, an arcade shooter, but the multiplayer formula still works best when there’s time to recoup and recover, make tactical flanks and call in your scorestreaks.

Infinity Ward’s Modern Warfare 4 removes the omnimovement system, but it still allows players to sprint, slide and dolphin dive around at appreciably high speeds. The new mantling mechanic adds some traversal options, but everyone feels a little heavier.

The slightly slower six-versus-six matches feel great, and the larger modes are a bit less chaotic. The Modern Warfare games have always skewed closer to classic boots-on-the-ground Call of Duty, and the latest entry doesn’t disappoint in that regard.

Still, the fatal flaws of the modern Call of Duty formula have gone untouched. There remain more than 70 attachments for many weapons. Many modes have maps cut out of larger Warzone areas. The seemingly mandatory 24/7 Shipment playlist is being added soon to prey upon your nostalgia. Progression needs to synergize across a complete Modern Warfare 4 product, so unnecessary bloat exists everywhere you look.

This is a solid modern Call of Duty game, but the overall quality is still a far cry from the series’ heyday. In a post-Warzone world, this is about as good as it gets — but if that formula doesn’t work for you, it might be worth steering clear of Modern Warfare 4.

articles.headline: Newey responds to Horner's 'abandon ship' criticism
keyFacts: Adrian Newey responded to claims in Christian Horner's new book that Newey wanted to abandon Red Bull during struggles in 2014.
Newey stated that Horner did not fully understand the pain and frustration he experienced regarding poor engine performance from supplier Renault.
Newey declined a Ferrari offer in 2014 to stay at Red Bull before eventually leaving the team a decade later.
body: Adrian Newey responds to Christian Horner's criticism of him in new book over Red Bull's struggles with Renault in 2014

In his autobiography, ex-Red Bull boss Christian Horner claims Adrian Newey" wanted to abandon ship" at "first sign of adversity" at team in 2014; watch every United States GP session live on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 10pm on Saturday and the race at 8pm on Sunday
Friday 23 October 2026 23:38, UK

Adrian Newey suspects Christian Horner did not "fully understand" his "pain and frustration" during Red Bull's fallow years with Renault engines after criticism of him in the former team principal's new book.

Horner as team principal and Newey as technical chief worked together with huge success across 19 years at Red Bull, enjoying two periods of sustained title-winning form with first Sebastian Vettel in 2010-2013 and then Max Verstappen in 2021-2024.
But between those periods Red Bull took a back seat to Mercedes' dominance of the sport following the arrival of turbo-hybrid engines in 2014.

Red Bull initially continued to be powered by Renault, as in their four title-winning years under the previous rules era, but the French manufacturer struggled with the new regulations, which compromised the performance of the team's Newey-designed car.

Writing in his newly-released autobiography, Drive, Horner recounted a period mid-way through 2014 when he became disappointed in Newey after the legendary designer had received an offer to join Ferrari and was mulling whether to leave.
Horner wrote: "I stood behind him and believed that he stood behind me as well. But at the first sign of adversity, Adrian wanted to abandon ship. I felt very sad about that."
Horner added that, despite Newey's importance to the team, "I could no longer rely on him. Our partnership was not as solid as I had previously believed."
Horner's comments were put forward to Newey in Friday's team principals' press conference at the United States Grand Prix.
"You're quite right in saying that, no, I haven't read any of it [the book] yet," replied Newey.
"I think 2014, as a chassis designer, if the PU [Power Unit] manufacturer has a bad year, that happens and you accept it.

"If the PU manufacturer has a bad year and doesn't appear to have any intention of trying to address the problem, that's altogether a different matter and that's quite bleak at that point. And that's the situation that unfortunately we faced in 2014.
"And as it turned out, that situation didn't really change with that supplier until we changed to Honda in 2019.
"So, you can imagine my pain and frustration at that. I don't think Christian fully understood that, perhaps. But I was in conversation."
Ultimately turning down Ferrari's offer in 2014, Newey signed a new contract to stay at Red Bull but began to split his time with other projects at the company outside of F1.
Newey stayed a further decade at Red Bull before leaving eventually in 2024 to join Aston Martin the following year, where he is team principal and managing technical partner.
Newey added: "The rest of it [in the book] I really can't comment, but Christian and I remain friends. As many of you know, I am godfather to his daughter Olivia, so, yeah."

In interviews publicising his book, Horner said he saw similarities between Newey's current experience of trying to turn around a struggling Aston Martin team to their early years at Red Bull following the energy drink's buyout of an underachieving Jaguar outfit in 2005.
It was a comparison that Newey agreed with.
"I think there are actually a lot of parallels between when I started at Red Bull and when I've started at Aston Martin," said Newey.
"Both teams that through their history had had quite a lot of turmoil with changes of owners, changes of senior managers, etcetera.
"It's then really trying to, as we've spoken before, get everybody working together, try to break down silos, improve the culture. And that's been exactly the same again."
Speaking to Sky Sports News earlier this week, Horner said: "Adrian is without doubt the best designer that Formula 1 has ever seen. His track record speaks for itself.

"Lawrence [Stroll] is a very successful guy. He's a very driven guy and has obviously invested heavily in that team. Honestly, I think they've got their own journey that they're on, and it'll be interesting to see how it plays out."
